chapters.title: Loads, equilibrium and graphic statics
chapters.summary: A building stands when every part of it is in equilibrium under its loads without its materials being overstressed. Forces add as arrows, so equilibrium can be drawn: the force polygon closes and the funicular polygon shows the shape a string would take under the same loads. With stress, strain and a factor of safety we have the vocabulary for everything that follows.

items.name: Loads: dead, live, snow and wind
items.pic: Stack loads onto a floor bay — self-weight, people, snow, a wind gust — and see the total reaction and its path down to the foundations, with each component coloured.

items.name: Static equilibrium of forces and moments
items.pic: Drag loads along a beam on two supports: the reactions update so that ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0, and a lever-arm overlay shows the moment balance.

items.name: Supports, free-body diagrams and determinacy
items.pic: Swap pin, roller and fixed supports under a beam: the count of unknown reactions against three equations flags the structure as a mechanism, determinate or indeterminate.

items.name: Force polygon (Stevin’s parallelogram)
items.pic: Draw forces acting at a point as arrows nose to tail: the closing side is the equilibrant, and dragging any force reshapes the polygon live.

items.name: The funicular polygon (Varignon)
items.pic: Pick a pole point in the force diagram: rays from it give segment directions of a string polygon under the loads; moving the pole changes the polygon’s depth but never its validity.

items.name: Tension, compression and bending
items.pic: Load a rope, a column and a plank: colour each by axial stress or bending, and see which shapes carry load by pure tension or compression.

items.name: Building materials compared
items.pic: Plot stone, brick, timber, steel, reinforced concrete and fabric on strength-versus-density and stiffness-versus-density charts, with each material’s good uses (compression, tension, bending) marked.

items.name: Load paths through a building
items.pic: Click a floor, roof or wall and follow its load down through slabs, beams, columns and foundations; remove a column and the load must find another path or the structure fails.

chapters.title: Cables and suspension structures
chapters.summary: A cable can only pull, so it takes up exactly the funicular shape for its loads: a polygon under point loads, a parabola under a uniform deck, a catenary under its own weight. Sag controls cable force, and that one relation shapes every suspension and cable-stayed bridge. Stiffening the deck against moving loads was the decisive engineering problem of the long-span era.

items.name: Cables under point loads take funicular shapes
items.pic: Hang weights from a cable and drag them: the cable relaxes into the funicular polygon of those loads, matching the graphic-statics construction.

items.name: Suspension cables under a uniform deck
items.pic: Hang a heavy deck from a light cable with many hangers: as the deck-to-cable weight ratio grows, the computed cable shape approaches the parabola, with the maximum deviation read out.

items.name: Parabola versus catenary
items.pic: Overlay a parabola and a catenary of equal span and sag: increase the sag ratio and the gap grows from invisible to obvious, with the deck-to-cable weight ratio deciding which fits.

items.name: Cable tension and sag: H = wL²/8d
items.pic: Slide the sag of a cable: horizontal tension soars as the cable flattens, and a cost curve for cable plus tower height shows an optimum near span/10.

items.name: The suspension bridge
items.pic: Assemble towers, main cables, hangers, deck and anchorages: load the deck and trace how forces travel to the anchorages and down the towers.

items.name: Deck stiffening against moving loads
items.pic: Drive a heavy truck across a suspension bridge with adjustable deck stiffness: a flexible deck sags under the truck, a stiff truss deck spreads the load to many hangers.

items.name: Cable-stayed bridges: fan and harp
items.pic: Toggle fan and harp stay layouts and tower height: stay forces and deck compression are computed and shown as line thickness.

chapters.title: Arches and the line of thrust
chapters.summary: Hooke saw that a hanging chain, turned upside down, gives the shape of an arch that stands in pure compression. In a masonry arch the line of thrust is the path of the internal compressive force; Heyman’s safe theorem says that if any such line fits inside the stones, the arch will stand. Masonry is thus a matter of geometry rather than strength, and buttresses, pinnacles and pointed arches are all ways of keeping that line inside the masonry.

items.name: Hooke’s inversion applied to masonry design
items.pic: Hang a chain with weights matching an arch’s voussoirs, then flip it: the inverted shape carries the same loads in pure compression; add or move weights as Hooke, Poleni and Gaudí did.

items.name: Line of thrust
items.pic: Cut an arch at any joint: the resultant force across the cut is drawn, and its points of application trace the thrust line through the arch.

items.name: Voussoirs, keystone and centering
items.pic: Build an arch stone by stone on timber centering: it cannot stand until the keystone is placed, after which striking the centering leaves it standing.

items.name: Heyman’s assumptions for masonry
items.pic: Toggle each assumption — no tensile strength, unlimited compressive strength, no sliding — and see which failure modes it rules out on a loaded arch.

items.name: Heyman’s safe theorem
items.pic: Drag the thrust line’s horizontal force and its end points: whenever some line fits inside the masonry the arch is declared safe, and the minimum and maximum thrust are marked.

items.name: Hinges and the four-hinge collapse mechanism
items.pic: Load an arch at the quarter point until the thrust line touches the edge at four places: hinges open there and the arch collapses as a four-bar linkage.

items.name: Minimum thickness of a semicircular arch
items.pic: Compare a canonical continuous annular-sector thrust calculation with the nine printed Nikolić table entries; vary thickness through the full segmental-to-horseshoe range and inspect the numerical clearance and transition.

items.name: Spreading supports and cracking are not failure
items.pic: Let the abutments spread a little: three hinges crack open, the thrust line jumps to the minimum, yet the arch stands until the spread becomes gross.

items.name: Buttresses: bringing the thrust to the ground
items.pic: Vary the width and height of a pier under a fixed symmetric arch; inspect the finite toe moment, why taller can be worse, and the separately proved maximum-thrust bound for this authored example.

items.name: Flying buttresses and pinnacles
items.pic: Vary imposed strut thrust, pier width and centred top weight in an authored plane section; check the exact outer-toe condition at every horizontal cut, with explicit omissions.

items.name: Pointed versus round arches
items.pic: Morph an arch from semicircular to pointed: horizontal thrust falls, and a point load at the crown fits better inside the pointed shape.

items.name: Medieval rules of proportion for buttresses
items.pic: Reconstruct the equal-arc buttress construction inspected in Huerta’s reproduced Derand diagram, then compare its proportion with a separate imposed-load rectangular-pier benchmark.

items.name: A Description of Helioscopes, and Some Other Instruments

paper.title: A Description of Helioscopes, and Some Other Instruments
paper.venue: London, p31, invention 2; Waller, Life of Hooke (1705), pxxi

items.pic: Invert an exact 24-link massless polygon carrying 23 equal node weights, bump a vertical envelope, and test analytically whether any funicular for those same weights fits; inspect Waller’s deciphered Latin with a registered control.

items.name: The Stone Skeleton

paper.title: The stone skeleton
paper.venue: International Journal of Solids and Structures 2 (2): 249–279

items.pic: Inspect Heyman’s no-tension joint yield wedge and the finite-crushing parabolic boundary from Fig. 2; vary axial load and eccentricity, reconstruct a compressive contact-pressure witness, and distinguish this local test from the whole-structure safe theorem.

chapters.title: Vaults and domes
chapters.summary: Vaults extend the arch into space, and domes extend it around a vertical axis. A dome carries load by meridional compression and by hoop forces that turn to tension low down, which is why masonry domes crack along meridians and why their builders used chains, rings and thickened haunches. From the Pantheon to Brunelleschi to modern thrust-network analysis, the same equilibrium reasoning applies.

items.name: Barrel and groin vaults
items.pic: Compare the open-edge groin geometry and barrel surface, with explicit conditional corner-weight and wall-strip models; wall openings have no safety calculation.

items.name: Rib vaults and the Gothic skeleton
items.pic: Vary the web weight and rib depth in a 24-block diagonal plane model; test one prescribed thrust candidate without inferring a unique 3D load path or collapse.

items.name: Membrane theory of domes
items.pic: A hemispherical shell under self-weight: meridional and hoop forces are plotted along the meridian, with compression blue and tension red.

items.name: Hoop tension below 51.8° in a hemisphere
items.pic: Slide down the meridian of a hemispherical dome: the hoop force changes sign at 51.8° from the crown, and a dome truncated above that line is compression-only.

items.name: Meridional cracking and the dome as sliced arches
items.pic: Let the lower hoops crack: the dome divides into wedge-shaped arches, and each slice’s thrust line is checked inside its thickness.

items.name: Poleni’s hanging-chain analysis of St Peter’s (1748)
items.pic: Read the original50-sector/16-bead construction and literal TableAA ratios; compare an exact authored point-load funicular with its inversion and a restricted reference band, with separate finite-polygon hoop equilibrium.

items.name: The Pantheon: step rings, coffers and graded concrete
items.pic: Compare complete piecewise spherical weight-resultant curves with one-sided load jumps; distinguish the authored mass laws from the original intact/cracked finite-element study and real-building safety.

items.name: Brunelleschi’s dome in Florence
items.pic: Distinguish the historic octagonal double shell from an authored circular-shell family; compare complete hoop curves, exact positive band integrals and a separate local block-friction inequality.

items.name: Pendentives: a dome on a square
items.pic: Construct exact spherical patches within four side planes, compare analytic curved and projected areas, and test a trial circle against the fixed crown joint without a structural safety inference.

items.name: Compression rings, oculi and lanterns
items.pic: Open an oculus at the crown: the meridional forces must be gathered by a compression ring, and adding a lantern’s weight changes the thrust lines below.

items.name: Thrust network analysis
items.pic: Edit a horizontal force network over a vault plan and its reciprocal diagram: the solver finds heights that place a compression-only network inside the vault’s thickness.

chapters.title: Beams, columns and trusses
chapters.summary: Beams carry load through a signed bending-stress field, while matching funicular forms and trusses can use axial force. Chosen stress, stiffness, geometry and support assumptions control every comparison. Rigidity is tested by actual first-order rank, not bar counts alone; a globally shared reciprocal connects joint equilibrium with a force diagram. Finite authored calculations are teaching models, not safety assessments of historical structures.

items.name: The moment diagram is a funicular polygon
refs: Written ARCH1.2/1.5; supplied cut-equilibrium derivation; MIT2.080 Lecture 5 Eqs.5.3–5.4
items.pic: Change the load, its position, distributed loading and H. Compare the computed moment with −H times the actual funicular ordinate.

items.name: Structural depth and span-to-depth ratios
refs: MIT2.080 Lecture 4 Eqs.4.23–4.30; Lecture 5 beam equation and supplied central-load integration
items.pic: Vary span, depth, load and chosen elastic constants. Read both stress and serviceability requirements instead of treating a span/depth ratio as a guarantee.

items.name: Form-active versus bending-active structures
refs: Supplied joint-equilibrium and stress-volume derivations; MIT2.080 Lecture 4 bending stress
items.pic: Hold the central load and allowed stress fixed while changing span and structural depth. Compare the actual conditional volumes and the omitted support/buckling costs.

items.name: Galileo’s cantilever problem (1638)
refs: BCIT Civil Engineering eduFacts, Galileo; J. X. Wang, Decision Making Under Uncertainty, publisher preview §1.1 pp.1–3; supplied moment integrals; MIT2.080 Lecture 4
items.pic: Compare the two section stress assumptions and their predicted nominal tip-load limits. Change depth and length to see the common square-depth/inverse-length scaling.

items.name: Columns: from the classical orders to steel
refs: MIT2.080 Lecture 9 §9.2, Eqs.9.34–9.37; supplied endpoint calculation
items.pic: Change length, square side, chosen modulus/compression limit and end condition. Compare Euler and compression limits on the positive log-load axis; the mode shape is normalized rather than a predicted postbuckling displacement.

items.name: Maillart’s deck-stiffened arches
refs: JHU Perspectives, Schwandbach Bridge entry; ASCE Salginatobel Bridge; supplied positive quadratic compatibility model
items.pic: Change relative deck stiffness, connector stiffness and load position. Observe the compatible displacement amplitudes and computed restoring-force shares.

items.name: Triangulation and trusses
refs: Connelly et al. 2009 §2.1, compatibility/equilibrium matrices; supplied exact rhombus family
items.pic: Fold the actual unbraced square while its side lengths remain fixed. Add the diagonal and compare computed rigidity rank; the fold control then disappears.

items.name: Funicular trusses: chords shaped to the moment
refs: ETH eQUILIBRIUM constant-force chord examples; supplied nodal equilibrium and direct-stiffness model
items.pic: Switch the lower chord between funicular and flat, add an unmatched first-node load, and inspect the actual signed diagonal forces and equilibrium residual.

items.name: Maxwell–Cremona reciprocal diagrams
refs: Van Mele & Block 2014 §§2.1–2.2; supplied complete four-vertex reciprocal
items.pic: Change roof rise, apex position and load, then highlight each joint polygon. Compare paired directions, the shared force vertices and the external load line.

items.name: Maxwell’s rule for rigid frameworks
refs: Connelly et al. 2009 §2.1; supplied planar rank-nullity derivation
items.pic: Compare an unbraced square, one diagonal, two diagonals and a count-passing degenerate geometry. Read actual rank, mechanisms and self-stress rather than using a count as a certificate.

items.name: Truss types: Pratt, Howe, Warren and bowstring
refs: MIT public truss/direct-stiffness teaching context; supplied axial-energy assembly and equilibrium
items.pic: Switch actual topologies and change depth/load. Compare computed tension/compression and all four equal-load stress-volume proxies.

items.name: Space frames and geodesic domes
refs: Connelly et al. 2009 §2.1,3D count; supplied icosahedral subdivision and3D rigidity calculation
items.pic: Change subdivision, height and viewing angle, or compare a braced/unbraced tetrahedron. Inspect actual 3D rank and boundary mechanisms beside the labelled orthographic projection.

items.name: Cantilever bridges and the Forth Bridge model
refs: Princeton CASCE, Human Cantilever Model; supplied one-side free-body balance
items.pic: Change inner/outer arm lengths and suspended load. Trace the resulting pier and anchorage forces and test the equal-arm special case.

items.name: Prestressed concrete
refs: MIT2.080 Lecture 4 Eqs.4.23–4.30; supplied eccentric-force equilibrium and linear superposition
items.pic: Move the tendon, change effective force and applied moment, and inspect both extreme stresses and the chosen tensile-limit crossing.

items.name: On Reciprocal Figures and Diagrams of Forces
refs: Van Mele & Block 2014 §§2.1–2.2; supplied modern finite construction; Maxwell 1864 metadata only
items.pic: Change the roof geometry and load and highlight each closed joint polygon in the shared reciprocal. Read the actual forces and the displayed force/P coordinates, and compare the external load line.

paper.title: On Reciprocal Figures and Diagrams of Forces
paper.venue: The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science 27 (182): 250–261

chapters.title: Shells, membranes and form-finding
chapters.summary: Thin curved surfaces carry load through their shape, not their thickness, which lets a few centimetres of concrete span tens of metres. Saddle surfaces such as the hyperbolic paraboloid are both easy to build from straight lines and stiff; tensile membranes and cable nets must be anticlastic to stay taut. Because good shapes are hard to guess, designers from Gaudí to Frei Otto found them with hanging models and soap films, and engineers now do the same with computers.

items.name: Shells: strength from curvature
items.pic: Load a flat plate and a curved shell of the same thickness: the plate bends far more, while the shell carries the load by in-plane membrane forces.

items.name: The hyperbolic paraboloid
items.pic: Sweep a straight line along two skew lines to generate a hypar; rotate it to see both rulings and the arch and cable directions, as in Candela’s shells.

items.name: Anticlastic surfaces and tensile membranes
items.pic: Pretension a fabric between masts and anchors: only surfaces curving opposite ways in two directions stay taut, and a flat region flutters in the wind simulation.

items.name: Minimal surfaces and soap-film models
items.pic: Stretch a simulated soap film between draggable wire frames: it relaxes to zero mean curvature, reproducing the forms Frei Otto used for the Munich Olympic roofs.

items.name: Hanging models (Gaudí, Isler)
items.pic: Hang a net of strings with weights, as Gaudí did for the Colònia Güell, then invert it: the resulting vault is compression-only under the modelled loads.

items.name: Force-density method for cable nets
items.pic: Set a force-to-length ratio on each cable of a net and solve the linear system: changing densities reshapes the net, with equilibrium residuals shown at every node.

items.name: Dynamic relaxation
items.pic: Start a gridshell or membrane from a flat mesh and let pseudo-dynamics with damping settle it into equilibrium, with the kinetic-energy trace dropping to zero.

items.name: Gridshells
items.pic: Lift a flat lattice of timber laths into a doubly curved shell, as at Mannheim (1975): the lattice shears to fit, and bracing makes it stiff.

items.name: Tensegrity
items.pic: A three-strut tensegrity prism: struts float without touching, held by cables; slacken one cable and the structure collapses, tighten it and pretension stiffens it.

items.name: Pneumatic structures and the Laplace–Young relation
items.pic: Inflate a membrane over a span: internal pressure balances tension times curvature, Δp = T(1/R₁ + 1/R₂), and lowering pressure lets snow load dent the roof.

items.name: Thinness of shells: span-to-thickness ratios
items.pic: Compare span-to-thickness ratios of the Pantheon, a Candela hypar, an Isler shell and an eggshell; the buckling knockdown factor sets how thin each can safely be.

chapters.title: Scale, height and dynamics
chapters.summary: Weight grows with the cube of size but strength only with the square, so large structures must change shape rather than merely grow. Tall buildings are governed by wind and earthquakes, which turn statics into dynamics: every structure has natural frequencies, and loads that match them are dangerous. Tacoma Narrows and the London Millennium Bridge show two different ways a moving load and a structure can feed each other.

items.name: The square–cube law (Galileo)
items.pic: Scale a bridge or an animal bone by a factor k: weight grows as k³, cross-section as k², and the stress readout crosses the material limit at a computable size.

items.name: Tall buildings: lateral load and the framed tube
items.pic: Push a tall building with wind: compare drift for a rigid frame, a braced core and a perimeter tube, and see why steel per storey jumps with height for frames.

items.name: The Eiffel Tower’s profile
items.pic: Compute the shape whose legs point along the resultant of weight and wind at every height: the curve matches the tower’s splayed silhouette.

items.name: Natural frequencies of buildings
items.pic: Model a building as stacked masses on springs: its fundamental period grows with height (roughly N/10 s for N storeys) and the mode shapes sway on screen.

items.name: Earthquake response and resonance
items.pic: Shake a row of buildings of different heights with a recorded ground motion: those whose period matches the ground’s dominant period sway most, as in Mexico City 1985.

items.name: Base isolation
items.pic: Insert flexible bearings under a building: its period lengthens past the earthquake’s energetic band, and floor accelerations drop on the response spectrum.

items.name: Tuned mass dampers
items.pic: Hang a pendulum mass near the top of a tower and tune its frequency: the main resonance peak splits and flattens, as with Taipei 101’s 660-tonne sphere.

items.name: Vortex shedding and the Strouhal number
items.pic: Blow wind past a chimney: vortices peel off alternately at f = St·U/D, and when f meets the chimney’s frequency it locks in and oscillates.

items.name: Tacoma Narrows collapse (1940)
items.pic: A shallow, flexible deck in steady wind: the twisting mode grows through aeroelastic flutter (negative aerodynamic damping), not because gusts matched a frequency; deepen the deck to stop it.

items.name: The Millennium Bridge wobble (2000)
items.pic: Walkers adjust their gait to a swaying deck: beyond a critical crowd size their footfalls synchronise and the lateral sway grows, until dampers are switched on.

chapters.title: Room acoustics
chapters.summary: A room shapes sound through its reflections. How long sound lingers depends on volume and absorption, as Sabine discovered when fixing a Harvard lecture hall, and concert halls are designed around his formula. Geometry adds its own effects: parallel walls produce flutter, concave surfaces focus sound into hot spots, and curved galleries carry whispers around their rim.

items.name: Direct sound, reflections and image sources
items.pic: Place a source and listener in a room plan: mirror-image sources generate the reflection paths, and the resulting echogram shows each arrival’s delay and strength.

items.name: Designing reverberation time with Sabine’s formula
items.pic: Choose a hall’s volume, seats and finishes: RT60 = 0.161 V/A is computed and compared with targets for speech, chamber music and organ, as for Boston Symphony Hall (1900).

items.name: Eyring’s correction for absorbent rooms
items.pic: Raise the average absorption coefficient: Sabine’s formula overestimates RT60 and even predicts reverberation in an open-air room, while Eyring’s logarithmic version goes to zero.

items.name: Flutter echoes between parallel walls
items.pic: Clap between two parallel walls: the impulse response is a rapid train of echoes at spacing 2d/c; tilt one wall by a few degrees and the train breaks up.

items.name: Whispering galleries (Rayleigh)
items.pic: Launch rays at grazing angle in a circular gallery like St Paul’s: they creep around the wall and stay close to it, so a whisper arrives clearly on the far side.

items.name: Focusing by domes and concave walls
items.pic: Ray-trace reflections from a dome or an elliptical room: energy concentrates at foci, creating the hot spots and dead spots that plague domed halls.

items.name: Room modes and the bass problem
items.pic: Change a room’s proportions: axial, tangential and oblique mode frequencies are listed and plotted, and clumped modes produce uneven bass at the listening seat.

items.name: Shoebox and vineyard halls
items.pic: Compare early reflections in a narrow shoebox hall and a fan-shaped hall: the shoebox delivers more lateral reflections, which listeners associate with spaciousness.

items.name: Chirped echo from a stepped pyramid
items.pic: Clap in front of a staircase like El Castillo’s: reflections from successive steps arrive at increasing intervals, and the spectrogram of the computed echo shows a falling chirp.

items.name: The mass law of sound insulation
items.pic: Double a wall’s mass per area or the frequency: transmission loss rises by about 6 dB, and a flanking path or a gap caps the achievable insulation.

chapters.title: Sun, light and climate
chapters.summary: Buildings sit under a sun whose path through the sky can be computed for any place and date. That geometry decides where shadows fall, how deep an overhang must be to shade summer windows but admit winter sun, how much heat a façade receives and how far daylight reaches into a room. Ancient builders aligned monuments with solstice sunrises using the same geometry.

items.name: The sun’s path: altitude and azimuth
items.pic: Choose latitude, date and time: the sun’s position is computed from declination and hour angle and drawn on a sky dome and a sun-path diagram.

items.name: Shadows and the sundial
items.pic: A gnomon’s shadow sweeps across a plaza as time runs: tilt the gnomon to the latitude and the hour lines become evenly spaced.

items.name: Overhangs and solar shading
items.pic: Size an overhang above a south window: the shaded fraction of the glass is plotted over the year, full in midsummer and nearly zero in midwinter.

items.name: Solar gain and Lambert’s cosine law
items.pic: Rotate and tilt a façade: incident solar flux is S·cos θ, integrated over a day for each orientation, showing why west windows overheat in summer afternoons.

items.name: Daylight factor and window design
items.pic: Change window height and room depth: a daylight-factor map across the floor shows light falling off with distance, and raising the window head pushes it deeper.

items.name: Solar alignments in monuments
items.pic: Set the date to the winter solstice at Newgrange: the computed sunrise azimuth lines up with the roof box and the beam reaches the chamber, and drifts away weeks later.

items.name: Thermal mass and the daily temperature lag
items.pic: Drive a heavy masonry wall and a light wall with the same daily outdoor temperature cycle: the heavy wall delays and damps the indoor swing, computed by a heat-diffusion model.

items.name: Stack ventilation and wind catchers
items.pic: Warm air rising in a tall shaft draws cooler air through low openings: airflow is computed from the height and temperature difference, with a wind-catcher variant.
